items.title: Lexplain – AI-powered Linux kernel change explanations
items.raw_excerpt: To understand what changed between kernel versions, you have to dig through the git repository yourself. Commit messages rarely tell you the real-world impact on your systems — you need to analyze the actual diffs with knowledge of kernel internals. For engineers who use Linux — directly or indirectly — but aren't kernel developers, that barrier is pretty high. I kept finding out about relevant changes only after an issue had already hit, and it was most frustrating when the version was too new to find similar cases online. I built lexplain with the idea that it would be nice to quickly scan through kernel changes the way you'd skim the morning news. It reads diffs, analyzes the code, and generates two types of documents: - Commit analyses: context, code breakdown, behavioral impact, risks

items.title: Origin – Git blame for AI agents (track which AI wrote every line)
items.raw_excerpt:
We built Origin after realizing nobody on our team could answer "which AI wrote this?" when a bug appeared. Origin hooks into Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini, and Codex. Every commit gets tagged with which agent wrote it, what prompt generated it, which model, and what it cost. Run `origin blame` on any file and you see [AI] or [HU] per line — like git blame but for AI agents. All data stored in git notes. No server required, works offline, zero lock-in. CLI is open source (MIT): github.com/dolobanko/origin-cli
Team dashboard: getorigin.io Would love feedback on the attribution approach — we're using git notes to store session data on commit hashes.

items.title: 人类在 AI 辅助软件开发中应扮演何种角色？
items.raw_excerpt: Martin Fowler 博客中，Kief Morris 探讨了 AI 辅助开发中人的角色，认为开发者不会完全脱离开发流程，未来更多会以 “在循环之上” 的模式工作，通过制定规范、测试与反馈机制来指导 AI 智能体，而非逐一审查 AI 生成的内容。

title_i18n.zh: 人类在 AI 辅助软件开发中应扮演何种角色？
title_i18n.en: What role should humans play in AI-assisted software development?
title_i18n.es: ¿Qué papel debe desempeñar el ser humano en el desarrollo de software asistido por IA?

excerpt_i18n.zh: Martin Fowler 博客中，Kief Morris 探讨了 AI 辅助开发中人的角色，认为开发者不会完全脱离开发流程，未来更多会以 “在循环之上” 的模式工作，通过制定规范、测试与反馈机制来指导 AI 智能体，而非逐一审查 AI 生成的内容。
excerpt_i18n.en: In Martin Fowler's blog, Kief Morris discusses the role of humans in AI-assisted development, arguing that developers will not be completely removed from the development process. Instead, they will increasingly work in an "over the loop" mode, guiding AI agents by setting standards, tests, and feedback mechanisms, rather than reviewing each piece of AI-generated content individually.
excerpt_i18n.es: En el blog de Martin Fowler, Kief Morris analiza el papel de los humanos en el desarrollo asistido por IA, argumentando que los desarrolladores no se desvincularán completamente del proceso de desarrollo. En el futuro, trabajarán más en un modelo "sobre el bucle", guiando a los agentes de IA mediante la definición de estándares, pruebas y mecanismos de retroalimentación, en lugar de revisar minuciosamente cada contenido generado por la IA.

excerpt_i18n.en: On March 18, a price increase announcement from Alibaba Cloud stirred waves in the cloud computing industry. More significant than the "price hike" itself, however, was the signal it sent: after years of price wars, cloud providers have begun systematically passing cost pressures to the market for the first time. Thus, an AI-driven "computing power price surge" has resonated globally. "If we don’t raise prices, costs will become unsustainable," an industry insider long focused on the cloud sector told Leifeng.com. Over the past year, the explosion of AI applications has pushed demand for computing power to unprecedented heights, while supply—including GPU capacity, data centers, and electricity—has struggled to keep pace. With demand growing exponentially and supply still constrained by physical limits, price has become an inevitable variable. Notably, this is not a uniform price increase. Facing similar cost pressures, different domestic cloud providers are making divergent choices: some are adjusting only AI-related services while leaving core offerings untouched, others are implementing across-the-board hikes, and some are holding prices steady, aiming to capture market share through competitive pricing. "If we don’t raise prices, everyone’s costs will become unsustainable." "Everyone in the industry knew this wave of price increases was inevitable," cloud sales representative Zhang Xiangyu told Leifeng.com. In his view, this is not an active choice by cloud providers but rather a passive adjustment. Changes on the demand side are the most direct driver.

excerpt_i18n.en:
At the start of this year, global software stock investors collectively experienced a "terrifying sixty days." From the end of last year to the beginning of this year, the market was still immersed in the illusion of an "AI application explosion." However, at the end of January, Anthropic unveiled Claude Cowork, capable of autonomously operating computers and handling office tasks, which directly shattered the valuation logic of traditional SaaS. In just two months, North American software stocks lost over $1.6 trillion in market value. A nearly desperate sentiment pervaded the market: if AI can already operate computers and take over business workflows like humans, have the graphical interfaces and business software painstakingly built over the past two decades become outdated productivity tools? Addressing these life-or-death questions, in an online roundtable hosted by Leiphone GAIR Live, three industry veterans with deep expertise in SaaS and complementary perspectives—He Run: Co-founder and CEO of Zhi Qu Bai Chuan; Daniel: Senior investor and business head at a major internet company; Wu Hao: Author of "SaaS Entrepreneurship Roadmap," angel investor in leading SaaS companies, and former executive president—engaged in a rigorous 90-minute dialogue, offering penetrating insights into the current state and future of SaaS.  
1. Recent Plunge in SaaS Stock Prices: Not Due to Financial Revenue, but Expectations Being Dimensionality-Reduced  
In Daniel's view, the sharp decline in SaaS is not due to SaaS companies' financial data falling short of expectations, but rather expectations being subjected to a dimensionality-reducing blow.
excerpt_i18n.es: A principios de este año, los inversores en acciones de software a nivel global experimentaron juntos una "aterradora sesenta días". Desde finales del año pasado hasta principios de este, el mercado aún estaba inmerso en la ilusión de la "gran explosión de aplicaciones de IA". Sin embargo, a finales de enero, Anthropic lanzó Claude Cowork, capaz de operar computadoras de forma autónoma y realizar tareas de oficina independientes, lo que directamente destrozó la lógica de valoración del SaaS tradicional. En solo dos meses, las acciones de software en Norteamérica perdieron más de 1.6 billones de dólares en valor de mercado. El mercado se impregnó de un discurso casi desesperado: si la IA ya puede operar computadoras como un humano y hacerse cargo de los flujos de negocio, entonces, ¿para qué sirven las interfaces gráficas y los procesos comerciales que hemos construido con tanto esfuerzo en las últimas dos décadas?

items.title: AI Roundtable – Let 200 models debate your question
items.raw_excerpt: Hey HN! After the Car Wash Test post got quite a big discussion going (400+ comments, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47128138 ), I spent the past few weeks building a tool so anyone can run these kinds of questions and get structured results. No signup and free to use. You type a question, define answer options, pick up to 50 models at a time from a pool of 200+, and they all answer independently under identical conditions. No system prompt, structured output, same setup for every model. You can also run a debate round where models see each other's reasoning and get a chance to change their minds. A reviewer model then summarizes the full transcript. All models are routed via my startup Opper. Any feedback is welcome! Hope you enjoy it, and would love to hear what you think!
